content: The Guidelines for the Prevention, Diagnosis, Care, and Treatment of People with Chronic Hepatitis B Infection were published by the World Health Organization (WHO) in March 2024. These guidelines are available in both electronic and print formats, with respective ISBNs 978-92-4-009090-3 and 978-92-4-009091-0. The WHO permits the use, adaptation, and redistribution of this work for non-commercial purposes, provided proper citation is given. However, the use of the WHO logo is prohibited, and any adaptations must be licensed under the same or an equivalent Creative Commons license. If a translation is created, it must include a disclaimer stating that the translation was not produced by WHO and that the original English version remains the authoritative edition. The guidelines emphasize that WHO does not endorse any specific organizations, products, or services mentioned within the document. The publication includes a general disclaimer that the designations and material presented do not imply any opinion on the legal status of countries, territories, or boundaries. WHO has taken all reasonable precautions to verify the information provided, but the material is distributed without any warranty, either expressed or implied. The document includes acknowledgments of contributions from numerous experts and organizations. The Guidelines Development Group was chaired by Wendy Spearman (University of Cape Town, South Africa) and Saeed Sadiq Hamid (Aga Khan University, Pakistan), with Roger Chou (Oregon Health and Science University, USA) serving as the guidelines methodologist. The group included experts from various countries and institutions, representing a wide range of expertise in hepatitis B and related fields. The guidelines also benefited from systematic reviews and meta-analyses conducted by researchers from institutions such as the UCL Institute of Liver and Digestive Health (UK), Institut Pasteur (France), and others. These reviews covered topics such as the diagnostic accuracy of non-invasive fibrosis tests, the natural history of chronic hepatitis B, the efficacy of antiviral therapy, and the cost-effectiveness of prophylaxis during pregnancy. The document outlines key terms and concepts related to hepatitis B, including the phases of infection (immune-tolerant, immune-active, inactive, and immune-escape phases), serological markers (e.g., HBsAg, HBeAg, anti-HBs, anti-HBe), and complications such as cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). It also describes diagnostic and monitoring tools, such as alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), and HBV DNA quantification. The guidelines address specific populations, including children, adolescents, and pregnant women, and provide recommendations for expanded treatment eligibility, research priorities, and implementation considerations. They also highlight the importance of addressing co-infections with hepatitis D virus (HDV) and the role of laboratory-based and point-of-care testing in improving diagnosis and treatment outcomes. Overall, the guidelines represent a comprehensive effort to provide evidence-based recommendations for managing chronic hepatitis B infection globally, with input from a diverse group of experts and stakeholders.
